title: Knives, saws and hand tools: useful skills, safe limits
tldr: Choose tools for a defined task, learn their instructions and keep cutting work separate from people. Tools are part of practical preparedness; they should not add avoidable injuries or become improvised weapons.
steps: Use a purpose-made tool of manageable size. Check handles, guards, locking mechanisms and condition; retire damaged equipment rather than relying on tape to restore safety.
Use stable footing, adequate light and a secure work surface. Keep other people away from the working area and stop when distracted or fatigued.
Use the correct sheath or guard. Secure tools during transport and keep them inaccessible to children. Do not leave blades loose in bags.
Get practical instruction for the actual task. Practice on suitable material in safe conditions before taking a tool on a trip.
sections: Start with the tools needed to maintain your existing equipment: suitable fasteners, manufacturer-approved repair materials, a small screwdriver set and a practical cutting tool if trained to use it. A larger blade or axe is not automatically more useful. Carrying weight, skill, permitted use and injury consequences all matter.

Check what is behind or under the material, who can enter the area and how a tool will be put down safely. Gloves may help for an appropriate task but do not make poor technique safe. Never improvise load-bearing repairs, cut live electrical equipment or use a tool in a way the manufacturer prohibits.
without_help: Stop the job if adequate light, footing or competent instruction is unavailable. Use a simpler existing solution or arrange qualified help; finishing a repair is not worth an avoidable serious injury.
household: Keep tools away from shared food and children’s bags. Choose accessible handles and suitable task roles rather than assuming everyone can safely use the same tool.
pack_now: Keep the equipment and written information described above where the responsible person can reach them. Test access in darkness, with a tired household, and while carrying the items you actually need.
next: Inspect a small tool kit, identify one damaged item and arrange a supervised lesson for one useful task.
watch: This guide does not cover combat use, weapon construction, traps or hazardous field surgery. Specific cutting techniques need practical instruction.
review_status: Source-linked editorial review; not independent expert certification
scope: Civilian educational planning. References include U.S. systems; local laws, conditions and services differ.
